name: Peter Lynch
summary:
Peter Lynch was born January 19, 1944, in Newton, Massachusetts. His father, an accountant, died of brain cancer when Lynch was a boy, and Lynch worked as a golf caddie from his early teens to help support the family — a job that, by his own account, gave him his first informal exposure to investors and executives. He attended Boston College partly on savings that included profits from an early stock purchase, studying history, psychology, and philosophy rather than finance, and later credited that broader background, especially training in logic, as better investing preparation than his business coursework. He earned an MBA from Wharton in 1968.

Lynch joined Fidelity Investments as an intern in 1966 through a connection made while caddying, became a permanent research analyst in 1969 after an Army stint, and served as Fidelity's director of research from 1974 to 1977. In 1977 he was named manager of the then-obscure Magellan Fund, holding about $18 million in assets. Over the thirteen years he ran it, until retiring in 1990, Magellan averaged a 29.2% annual return — consistently beating the S&P 500 — and grew to roughly $14 billion, a record widely cited as among the best in mutual fund history.

Lynch's investing philosophy, distilled in One Up on Wall Street and his later books, holds that individual investors can spot promising companies in everyday life before professional analysts do, provided they follow up with real research into fundamentals rather than acting on familiarity alone. He popularized the phrase "invest in what you know," coined the term "tenbagger" for a stock that returns tenfold, and helped popularize the growth-at-a-reasonable-price (GARP) approach. Since retiring from day-to-day management, he has remained part-time vice chairman of Fidelity Management & Research and devoted much of his time to philanthropy through the Lynch Foundation.
achievements: Managed Fidelity's Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, averaging a 29.2% annual return and growing it from $18 million to roughly $14 billion in assets — a record widely cited as among the best in mutual fund history
Wrote One Up on Wall Street and Beating the Street, popularizing the phrase 'invest in what you know' and the term 'tenbagger' for a stock that returns ten times its purchase price
Helped popularize the growth-at-a-reasonable-price (GARP) approach to stock selection, balancing growth potential against valuation discipline
Devoted decades to philanthropy through the Lynch Foundation, including a major gift to Boston College that led to the naming of its Lynch School of Education and Human Development

quotes.text: Know what you own, and know why you own it.
Although it's easy to forget sometimes, a share of stock is not a lottery ticket. It's part ownership of a business.

legacy: Lynch's Magellan Fund track record remains a reference point for what active fund management can achieve, and his plain-language investing philosophy — research ordinary companies you actually understand, rather than chase complexity — has shaped a generation of individual investors and financial writers who followed him. "Invest in what you know" and "tenbagger" both entered common investing vocabulary well beyond readers of his own books.
